patient.chief_complaint: Progressive gait deterioration and mild cognitive decline 14 months after bilateral subdural hematoma evacuation
patient.history_present_illness: A 74-year-old right-handed man with hypertension, atrial fibrillation, and bilateral chronic subdural hematomas (surgically evacuated 14 months ago via bilateral burr holes) was admitted for NPH evaluation. Post-operatively following his subdural evacuation, he had an acceptable recovery — cognitive function improved and he was ambulatory without assistance. However, over the past 8 months his gait has progressively deteriorated with increasing shuffling, wide-based gait, and two falls. He requires a walker. Cognitive performance has also declined gradually, though he remains able to manage daily activities with his wife's assistance. He has developed urinary urgency with occasional incontinence. His neurosurgical team has been monitoring him post-operatively and noted that repeat head CT shows hydrocephalus that was not present at 6-month post-operative CT — Evans index on current CT is 0.36. The neurosurgeon suspects secondary NPH (post-operative communicating hydrocephalus following subdural evacuation), a known complication. He is admitted for tap trial. Anticoagulation management is a safety concern for LP.

results.title: Secondary NPH after subdural evacuation — case series and outcomes
results.key_finding: Secondary NPH following subdural hematoma evacuation responds well to VP shunting with 70-80% improvement rates; better prognosis than idiopathic NPH

output.summary: Secondary NPH following subdural hematoma evacuation is a well-recognized complication, occurring in 1-5% of cases. The mechanism involves disruption of arachnoid granule CSF reabsorption during subdural pathology and surgery. VP shunt outcomes are generally favorable (70-80% improvement rate) — better than idiopathic NPH, likely because the underlying brain parenchyma is relatively preserved and there is no neurodegenerative copathology.
